Instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

Research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

No. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

In very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

#8796. 'I Ran 3 Miles A Day For 21 Days—Here's What I Learned About My Brain And Body'

Here’s what to expect, and how to commit.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There’s something romantic about the idea of a daily run. It’s simple. It’s gritty. It’s giving “I can do hard things just because I believe I can,” main character energy. Plus, running three miles a day has become a bit of a fitness trend lately—just scroll through TikTok and you’ll see thousands of people sticking to that sweet-spot distance to get in shape, clear their heads, or just establish a healthy daily habit.

I’ve dabbled in running over the years (mostly during half-hearted attempts to train for a 10K or half marathon), but I’ve never been consistent. So I challenged myself: Run (at least) three miles a day, every day, for three weeks—no skips. I wanted to see if this simple habit could actually deliver real results: Physically. Mentally. Emotionally. To cut to the chase, it did.

But before we dive into exactly what I learned, here’s what the challenge I set out for actually entailed: Each day, I carved out 30-ish minutes to run a minimum of three miles—sometimes on the treadmill, sometimes outside, depending on my mood (and the weather). Sometimes fast, sometimes slow—I wasn’t chasing speed, just consistency.

And while it started out as a little personal experiment, it turned into a full-on mindset shift that seeped into other areas of my life.

I’m a pretty high-energy person, even on little sleep. And frankly, when I’m not exerting that physical energy enough during the day, I find it tough to settle down to sleep at night.

By week two of this challenge, I was zonking out faster than usual and waking up feeling more rested. Research backs this up—moderate aerobic exercise like running can help you fall asleep quicker and improve sleep quality, per the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine.

There’s a reason running is considered a moving meditation (and I say this as someone who really struggles with stationary meditating). That ~30-minute mental break from work, life, communications, etc., helped me carve out time to shut off my brain and come back to reality with a fresh outlook.

Whatever I was stressing about before my run felt way less burdensome after taking time to move my body and just, well, not stress over that thing. I’d come back with more patience, more solutions, and frankly, a more can-do attitude about dealing with whatever was weighing me down before. My run became my reset button—and a way to make myself less irritable and more focused.

I’ve always gained (and lost) muscle pretty quickly after starting or stopping a new exercise routine, however I typically first notice it around my abs and arms, as I'm leaner in those regions. So, when I saw my calves and quads popping a bit more in the mirror, and climbing the four flights of stairs up to my apartment started feeling easier than it used to, I knew my body was adapting. Even though I wasn’t lifting weights during this three week challenge (I tried to at first, but decided it was too much for my schedule while also running three miles daily), the repeated use of lower-body muscles while running led to strength gains.

Going into this challenge, I expected a mental impact of some sort (though I wasn’t quite sure what it would be), but I didn’t think my body would change much from a short-distance, short-term running habit. I already work out often (switching it up with two to three weekly strength training sessions, yoga/pilates once per week, and a two to five mile run once per week), so I didn’t think this challenge would have a palpable physical effect on me. So, the lower body muscle and strength gains were by far the most surprising benefit I walked away with.

I’d never really consider myself a “runner,” but doing it daily for three weeks made the act feel less intimidating and more second nature to me. A study in Psychology of Sport and Exercise shows that consistency in movement creates more positive attitudes toward the habit, which makes you more likely to keep showing up. My experience totally backed that up.

Around day six, I felt myself gearing up for my run more instinctually—getting dressed, grabbing my headphones, keys, and lacing up my sneakers just right without having to think about it much. If on the first few runs I was moseying around the neighborhood walking for several blocks to put off actually starting the run, by week two I was excitedly hitting the pavement at my three-mile pace almost as soon as I got outside. Pacing myself began to feel more natural without checking my Nike Run Club app, and I started tapping into the sound of my feet hitting the concrete to gauge my effort.

Before this challenge, I had a habit of engaging in pretty critical self-talk on the regular. Also, mentally checking out mid-run was the norm in order to just get through it. My internal monologue when running used to be all about how much time was left, how uncomfortable I felt, or how nice it would feel to just stop. But sticking to a daily running habit triggered the kind of awareness and shift of self-talk that I’d been long overdue for. That mindset shift was probably the biggest win of all.

After a few days of three miles under my belt, I started celebrating tiny wins—like not stopping on a hill or picking up my pace on the final stretch. Instead of counting down the minutes or fixating on how slow I was moving, I was hyping myself up, which only propelled me further. Whether it was a solo sunset jog or a playlist-powered treadmill sesh, I always felt a little lighter—and a little more capable of not just enduring, but thriving through hard things—post-run. That energy and positive shift in self-talk started showing up in how I talked to myself outside of workouts, too.

It’s wild how one habit tends to have a domino effect, whether it’s constructive or destructive. Once I started running every day, I realized I wanted to support that effort outside of my run window. That meant reaching for water instead of a second coffee, getting in some light stretching at night, prioritizing protein in my meals, and actually winding down for sleep earlier than usual instead of binge-watching or doom-scrolling.

The momentum from running made other wellness choices feel less like chores and more like natural choices for self-care. I wasn’t trying to overhaul my entire routine overnight, but these little tweaks felt pretty intuitive, and really added up to help me stick with the challenge, and feel more energized and clear-headed throughout the day.

Okay, so full transparency: I didn’t just wake up one day and bust out 21 straight three-milers. I eased in by starting off slow to establish a new routine, and listening to my body along the way. Here’s how to start running three miles a day—without burning out.

Pro tip: “If you’re just starting out, alternate running days with walking or strength training to let your body adjust,” run coach Corky Corkum, CPT, previously told WH. “The number one reason new runners quit is injury or burnout from doing too much too soon.”

Want to try running three miles a day for yourself? These things made all the difference:

If your goal is to feel stronger, sleep better, and just feel a little more capable and confident—all with minimal equipment or cost—then yes, 100 percent. You don’t need a marathon medal to call yourself a runner or to be consistent. You just need a pair of sneakers, a bit of stick-to-it-ness, and a willingness to start where you are.

And if you happen to find yourself romanticizing the idea of making a daily jog a habit? I say lean into it.

But this year, we wanted to get more personal and spread some holiday cheer along the way. So the editors made a list of some of our most consistent writers and hand-selected gifts to match each of them. We sent the gifts to their doors and hoped we’d hit the mark.

And we are happy to share our IRL gift ideas with you for your own gifting or wish list creation. Below, you’ll find out a little bit more about some of our favorite contributors, what we gifted them, and why we think they’ll enjoy it.

About the contributor: Sara is lucky enough to live in the triathlete’s dream training locale: Kailua-Kona, Hawaii, home of the Ironman World Championship. Though there’s lots to envy, I’m particularly green over her access to daily open-water swimming. But I also worry because swimming in open water comes with more risks than the typical pool.

What we gifted (and why): Sara’s frequent open-water swimming is why I’m gifting her this safety buoy from Tri-Fit. It’s bright, so she’s visible to other swimmers and from shore, and stable in the water if she needs to use it to adjust her goggles or shake off a calf cramp. But wait, there’s more! What I really love about this buoy is that it goes beyond your standard safety product – it’s an actual training workhorse, with a 1-liter hydration bladder and bite valve for days when Sara decides she wants to swim with the dolphins and sea turtles a little longer.

What we gifted (and why): Life as a mom is busy and includes plenty of extras – like the armful of toys your child just has to bring with them to leave the house. As a fellow mom, I know what it feels like to not have enough arms to hold all the water bottles, snacks, and gear that comes with both triathlon and motherhood, so a bag with a pocket for everything can be a ready-made way of getting out of the house for training in an organized state, even when life as a mom feels far from organized.

About the contributor: Emma-Kate is a retired professional triathlete who’s still very much involved in the sport while continuing to multisport train and lift regularly. About the contributor: Tim is one of my favorite storytellers in triathlon, and I feel lucky to not only get to edit his stories regularly, but to hear the stories behind the stories. I can’t repeat most of them in print, but trust me when I say Tim Heming has seen some wild stuff.

#8793. 5 Yoga Poses That Help You Embody Gratitude

Calin Van Paris is a YJ editor and certified yoga instructor. Here, she shares five yoga poses that can help you access gratitude throughout your body—just in case you’re having a tough time feeling it in your heart.

The practice of gratitude can be a sticky subject. Certain events and times of year—season shifts, rites of passage, the holidays—prompt us to ponder the things in our lives that elicit gratitude. Life feels a little richer when experienced through the lens of gratitude.

But at times, accessing that gratitude can be easier said than done. Global happenings and situations in our individual lives aren’t always sunny or sparkly, and we don’t always feel grateful. Sometimes we’re just mad, sad, frustrated, or over it—even in November and December.

Rather than convincing your head (or heart) to be thankful, try feeling it in your body first. The following yoga poses can help transform the sometimes elusive concept of gratitude into something more physical.

Spend a few minutes in one of these poses contemplating  gratitude. The rest of you might follow.

There’s something worshipful about bowing on your knees, which makes Child’s Pose (Balasana) an easy choice for this list. When you’re in a grateful state, thanking the Universe can become akin to a prayer or mantra, one worth saying over and over again. Spend some time here, with your forehead and palms pressed to the earth, and imagine roots sprouting from all points of contact.

Another shape that finds you close to the earth, Squat (Malasana) is a pose of both humility and strength. Your feet planted on the ground offer stability, while the deep squat requires the cooperation of your entire lower body. Add the usual prayer hands, and Malasana becomes a demonstration of gratitude for your body, spirit, and anything else you choose to be grateful for.

When you imagine a full-body expression of joy, chances are the pose in your mind looks a lot like Upward Salute (Urdhva Hastasana). The act of standing strong and lifting your arms in celebration mirrors the instinctive expression of wholehearted gratitude. When you’re in an authentically grateful place, expressing it doesn’t feel like a chore or an obligation—it feels like a party.

Opening your heart can also begin in your body. Bending back in Camel Pose requires a certain amount of trust in your body as well as in gravity. Once you’ve found stillness in the pose, your heart and throat face upward in a way that’s both vulnerable and liberating. Embracing this shape is a physical prompt for you to revel in—and perhaps exude gratitude for—the human experience.

Lying prone on your back is perhaps the ultimate shape of surrender. Savasana finds your front body fully exposed to the Universe and all it has to offer while your back body roots you to the earth. Stilling your mind and body here demands an acceptance of this present moment, just as it is. And if that isn’t an expression of gratitude, then perhaps nothing is.

#8792. A Runner Took a Midrace Puff of Weed at the NYC Marathon. Now, She’s Disqualified.

This Houston attorney lost her official result, but kept her medal—and her sense of humor.

Having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral. Andrea Sager, though, has been getting some serious mileage out of the bad news on Instagram.

"Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.

The Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course. The moment she decided to accept a puff from a spectator was caught on video, and New York Road Runners subsequently removed her finish time from its records.

As far as the rules go, there's little room for debate. NYRR's Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits "smoking, vaping, or use of electronic smoking devices, tobacco products, or marijuana products" in the starting corrals, on the course, and in the finish area, with the restriction extending 1,000 feet beyond those locations.

In a video explaining her disqualification, Sager acknowledged breaking the rules and said she understood the decision. Even so, she claimed she wasn’t the only runner to drink alcohol or smoke weed during the race, and suggested the difference was having the moment seen by millions of people on social media.

"I wasn't planning on smoking weed on the course, but I was in so much pain and needed something to help me finish," she told the New York Post.

Sager hasn't let the penalty spoil her memories of race day. Her original finish-line recap described a grueling 26.2 miles that involved "approximately 47 mental breakdowns," although she was thrilled to check the race off her bucket list. She later reminded followers that the experience could not be taken away from her.

She'd been having plenty of fun long before arriving in New York, too. One prerace Instagram video joked about giving up dating apps in favor of training for a marathon, while her bright pink marathon shirt doubled as a personal advertisement. The front read, "Andrea, 35, Single. Great Credit. Bad Judgment," while the back added, "Looking for a man with more endurance than my ex."

Her latest social media introduction has since acquired another word: "35. Single. Great credit. Poor judgment. Disqualified."

Sager still has her finisher medal, and the extra attention has brought some unexpected opportunities.

"I'm talking with the brands now, so there's a lot of upside, but still annoying," she told the Post.

Sager said she was told she can participate in future NYRR events, despite the removal of her November 1 result. Runner's World contacted the organization for comment and confirmation of her eligibility but received no response.

As for racing plans, Sager said she has HYROX Houston on her calendar for April 2027. And someone in her Instagram comments has suggested a shirt idea for her next event:

"I smoked weed at the NYC marathon and all I got was a DQ."

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#8791. Procrastinating Your Winter Runs? Here’s What Will Actually Get You Out the Door, According to a Sports Psychologist

An expert explains which strategies work, what backfires in the long term, and when procrastination signals you need a training reassessment.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nine months of the year, I rarely struggle to get myself out the door for a run. Then winter arrives, the temperatures drop, and suddenly it’s three straight months of daily prerun procrastination: I look for any excuse, task, or chore to delay heading out into the cold or stepping on the treadmill.

While this does have occasional productivity benefits—my kitchen floor shines and my email inbox stays at zero—I’ll find myself more than an hour later no closer to starting my run. Except by then, I’m crunched for time, it’s pitch-black outside, and the whole process has drained enough of my mental energy that I’d rather push those miles to tomorrow.

I know I’m not alone: Even professional marathoners fall into the “run-crastination” spiral. Previously, Des Linden and Kara Goucher discussed their own experiences on their podcast, Nobody Asked Us with Des & Kara. Still, I’d much rather find a way to avoid getting sucked in so I can get on with my run and my day, and enjoy both a little more as a result.

So, I asked a sports psychologist what actually works to get you out the door in the winter when anything sounds better than a run—plus when it’s actually a better idea to skip the miles.

The first step to beating prerun procrastination? Determine the reason you’re doing it. “Procrastination is usually one of two things,” Justin Ross, Psy.D., a clinical sports psychologist and UESCA-certified run coach, tells Runner’s World. “One: It’s an avoidance strategy, because what you’re about to do is uncomfortable, unpleasant, hard, or challenging. But, it can also signal toward a different need that’s not being met.”

In the winter months—especially for driven runners coming off a fall marathon season—that other need can be rest. “True athletic wisdom is knowing the difference between when procrastination is avoidance, and when it’s a sign that you need something other than a run that day,” Ross explains.

Gaining that wisdom as an athlete takes time, practice, and some trial and error. The best way to start? Focus on creating “systems” that make procrastination less likely so you can more easily identify the action that aligns with your needs, goals, and values, Ross says. Most times, these systems (which we outline below) lead to better outcomes than trying to rely on willpower alone or following an impulse in the moment.

If you find yourself avoiding a run, remove as many obstacles as possible that stand between you and getting out the door or to the gym. For Ross, that means setting out all his running clothes and fuel ahead of time so he doesn’t need to hunt for that one pair of gloves he hasn’t seen since last January.

“Without preparation, procrastination becomes a whole lot easier because you have all these extra hurdles,” he explains. “When it’s dark and cold in the winter, you need to problem-solve in ways that you don’t need to when it’s beautiful out and you’re excited to run.”

For me, that means making sure my headlamp actually has working batteries if I’m planning to run outside in the evenings. If I’m hitting the treadmill, I cue up a playlist, TV show, or podcast on my phone and stock my gym bag with a postrun snack and a full water bottle.

When you’re procrastinating a run, try shifting your focus from what you’re doing to why you’re doing it. “Remind yourself why this run is important to you or how it helps you,” Ross says. For example, you might think about your values or current goals and consider how this workout brings you closer to them.

I’ve found I’m motivated simply by the fact that running makes me feel like my favorite version of myself—and that boosts my mood more than any race-specific or fitness goal. But you might be more excited by the idea that staying consistent with your training over the winter will set you up for a stronger chance at a marathon PR in the spring.

Consider what might add a little bit more spark to your routine or make it more enticing. You might decide to meet up with a friend or local run club for a few miles. You might look forward to your treadmill run as “the 30 minutes of my day where I don’t have to be bothered and I can just watch my favorite show [alone],” says Ross.

The reward mindset helps you refocus on what brings you joy, instead of just relieving the pressure of needing to get in a workout.

Another helpful strategy? Doing the absolute bare minimum. “Runners often fall into this trap of having rigid rules around their exercise or their training,” says Ross. Try letting go of whatever mileage or workout you had planned for the day, and tell yourself that you’ll just run for 10 minutes and then reassess how you feel.

You may even want to adjust your whole training standard ahead of the winter season, Ross says. For example, you might reduce the length, intensity, or frequency of the workouts you plan to do each week. Or, instead of targeting a specific pace or mileage requirement, run or cross-train solely based on time. “Think about being more flexible in your approach during the winter months. Maybe you aim for the minimal effective dose to get the benefit you’re looking for, like just running for 20 minutes if your usual standard is 60,” Ross suggests.

Ross explains that winter can be a meaningful time for runners to examine what rules they have around their training that might be adding pressure. For example, I used to follow a silly rule from an old college teammate who said that any run shorter than three miles “didn’t count” as a true run. Once I finally let go of that, I found it much easier to get moving—even if it was just for an easy walk in the park near my house.

“This time of year, see how you can approach exercise from an overall health or mood-boost perspective instead of a training perspective,” suggests Ross.

Also, question any rigid rules you’ve established for yourself around volume, pace, or mileage—like making sure to hit a specific number of miles every week or setting a minimum pace requirement for all your runs—because they may backfire and lead to mental burnout over the long term, he says.

If you’ve done all the above and you still can’t get yourself out the door, a run may not actually be what you need. “If you keep hitting the moment to head out and that intuitive voice says, ‘I just really don’t want to,’ try listening to that voice. Listen to your body,” Ross suggests. “It’s okay to give yourself permission for rest and recovery—especially during this time of year.”

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#8790. Fashion Has Entered Its Running Era

Luxury fashion brands have a thing for running shoes, apparently.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There was a time when you could spot someone who had just finished a run. They were sweaty and wearing sneakers that looked like they belonged exclusively on a track. These days, the shoes tell you almost nothing. That guy wearing carbon-plated racers might be heading out for a tempo run, or he might just be on his way to a bar or running errands (in a casual fit).

Running shoes have officially entered their fashion era, and while the whole sneaker-meets-streetwear thing isn't exactly new (the chunky dad sneaker era still lives rent-free in my head), the latest wave of collaborations feels a little different. Instead of reviving old silhouettes, fashion brands are getting their hands on actual performance shoes, and, frankly, some of the results are pretty damn good.

Take Adidas' collaboration with Satisfy, the Parisian running brand that's become something of a cult favorite among runners who lowkey like to look good while out and about. Earlier this year, the two brands gave the Adizero Adios Pro 4 a makeover, swapping its usual racing aesthetic for earthy tones, spray-painted details, and metallic accents. At first glance, they look like something you could spot on an edgy Instagram campaign, perhaps even a fashion week after-party in Bushwick, depending on the outfit. Except, it's still a legitimate racing shoe with Lightstrike Pro foam and EnergyRods. You could absolutely chase a PR in these. Whether you'd want to get them dirty is another question. That’s just merely scraping the surface, though.

Highsnobiety's latest collaboration with Saucony takes a similar approach, but with two very different sneakers: the Endorphin Pro 5, made for racing, and the ProGrid Paramount, a retro-inspired shoe that's more at home on city streets. Both get a modest makeover that makes technical sneakers look good with practically anything. Some of you probably appreciate the distinction here: one shoe is built for runners, and the other is for people who strictly care about style.

Then there's Hoka x Marni, which might be one of my favorites of the bunch. After giving the Bondi a ridiculously puffy, almost cartoonish makeover in 2025, the brands returned this November with the Clifton Marni, a more wearable take on Hoka's Clifton 11. There are metallic details, reflective accents, and a plaid sockliner, but underneath it all is still the cushioned daily trainer runners already know. It's stylish without looking like it's trying too hard, which can't be said for every designer sneaker collaboration.

Other brands have been getting in on the fun, too. Salomon and Pas Normal Studios recently put their spin on the Aero Blaze 4 GRVL, giving the gravel running shoe a sleek, outdoorsy look while keeping its GORE-TEX protection and trail-ready outsole. Aimé Leon Dore has brought its signature New York aesthetic to New Balance's FuelCell Rebel v5 and SC Elite v5, while Nike tapped designer Melitta Baumeister to reimagine the Vomero Premium and Pegasus Premium. Even Loewe and On are experimenting with high-fashion versions of technical running shoes. By now, the crossover is hard to ignore.

Of course, there's something funny about running, a sport that really doesn't require much beyond a decent pair of shoes (and your ability to actually run, of course), becoming another excuse to buy expensive, limited-edition sneakers. And not that this has to be said, but a designer collaboration isn't automatically a better running shoe. The fit, cushioning, and performance still matter, especially if you're planning to do more than walk around in them. But I do think it's cool that brands are putting this much thought into how performance footwear looks. Running clothes have gotten a lot more stylish in recent years, so why shouldn't the shoes follow?

#8789. Is Your AI Strength Plan Wasting Your Time? A Coach Weighs In

It’s not uncommon nowadays to ask AI to write your grocery list, design your kid’s birthday party invitation, and advise you on how best to taper before your next race, so we’re fairly certain there are a few triathletes out there asking Claude or Chat to draft a strength training program too.

Before you decide to do the same (or perhaps it’s too late and you already have), we thought we’d run an AI experiment where we ask a real human strength coach to assess the bot’s work to help decide how much of the plan is helpful for a multisport athlete, and how much would be a waste of time.

We asked ChatGPT for a strength routine suitable for a triathlete, and about four seconds later it returned a two-day plan complete with sets and reps.

Day one covered the lower body and core: squats or goblet squats, Romanian deadlifts, reverse lunges, standing calf raises, dead bugs, and side planks.

Day two went after the upper body and posterior chain: dumbbell bench press or push-ups, rows, lat pulldowns or assisted pull-ups, single-leg Romanian deadlifts, glute bridges or hip thrusts, and Pallof presses. The prescription included three sets of 8-10 reps, for 40 to 50 minutes per session, to be followed for 8-12 weeks.

It all looked perfectly sensible and not too dissimilar to what many triathletes do in most strength workouts. But for a triathlete who’s already squeezing three sports into one week, strength workouts should really be periodized and designed to augment what’s happening in the triathlete’s sport-specific training life (and the off-season is the one time of year when it’s great to do more in the gym, not less).

So with this in mind, we handed the plan to strength coach Sam Hengehold, who works with triathletes of all ages and abilities at Kinesis Integrated Performance in Boulder, Colorado. “I’d argue it is not right, but it’s also not wrong,” she says. “The plan is general, but it is not beneficial.”

Here’s the surprise: Hengehold wouldn’t strike a single exercise from the list.

“All exercises listed are actually great and could very well be integrated into a triathlete strength routine,” she says. “The limiter here is the lack of periodization and volume/load variables.”

Two of ChatGPT’s picks earn special praise:

Calf raises: “Many triathletes miss this integral exercise in their strength routine,” Hengehold says. “Lower leg injuries are extremely common with triathletes.” As a general rule, Hengehold wants athletes working toward calf raises at 1.5 times their body weight to build resiliency against injury in the calf, ankle, and foot.

Glute bridges: “A safe way to build power for beginners in strength training,” Hengehold says. They mostly train the glutes and core, the muscle groups that underpin all three disciplines.

So if the exercises are fine, where does the wasted time come in? It’s in how the plan asks you to do them.

To its credit, ChatGPT suggests lifting less often as race day approaches and adding a little load once the sets feel solid. But the exercises, sets, and reps never change. Your swim, bike, and run training is built in cycles around your races, and Hengehold advises that your lifting should be too.

In the off-season, strength work can take priority and endurance training becomes the base. In race season, that flips: Lifting is there to support your swim, bike, and run, and to keep your body resilient. A plan that looks identical in January and July does neither job well.

“Over time, it will just be an energy suck of a session, causing more fatigue in the athlete with minimal benefit,” Hengehold warns.

ChatGPT’s warm-up gets one line: 5-10 minutes of easy cardio, mobility, and lighter practice sets. Hengehold wants something more deliberate, with activation work chosen to prepare you for the main lift of the day.

“Warm-up and activation encourages proper form and oils the muscles,” Hengehold says. “Typically, that would include some sort of dynamic stretching, mobility, or preparation exercise that will aid in the main lift goals of the session. Before squats, for example, that might mean 90/90 hip rotations for hip mobility and banded clamshells to wake up the gluteus medius.” This matters if you want to avoid injury and get the most from every rep.

The big, complex lifts belong at the start of the session, when you’re fresh and can control your form. They also work better when paired with an athletic movement, Hengehold says, so the brain learns what the strength is for.

Follow loaded squats with box jumps, for instance, and you reinforce the power you need at toe-off on the run or when pushing watts on the bike. ChatGPT’s plan has no jumps and no explosive work at all.

“Neuromuscular understanding and adaptation is absolutely necessary for triathletes to maximize the benefit of strength training,” Hengehold says. Without it, you get some injury prevention and extra muscle mass, but not much else.

Hengehold named three categories of strength work that matter most for triathletes:

Core work: Think isometric holds and slow, controlled movements, with deep breathing throughout, to work the transverse abdominal muscles. Hengehold’s picks: planks with alternating shoulder taps, dead bugs, and bird dogs.

Unilateral movements: Single-leg Romanian deadlifts, Bulgarian split squats, front-foot elevated reverse lunges, and single-leg calf raises all make each side do its own share of the work. Swimming, biking, and running give a stronger side plenty of chances to cover for a weaker one, and these exercises help break those overcompensation patterns.

Squat variations: Isometric squats (holding the position) and eccentric squats (slowing the lowering phase) are a safe way to build resilience in the lower body and core. The squat is also endlessly adjustable, so it can be tweaked to target whatever you need most.

What you lift, and how, should depend on how far you are from your next race.

Far from race day: This is the time for heavy strength training alongside base swim, bike, and run work. Make complex lifts the centerpiece. Hengehold likes the trap bar deadlift. Get the form and technique down first, then spend a block (typically four to six weeks) building a base with high reps and low weight. Take a deload week, then switch to low reps and heavy weight to build real strength and durability.

In race season: Triathlon training takes over, and strength work drops to maintenance. Unilateral exercises move to the front, scheduled closely around your key sessions and races. Reps and load should go mostly on perceived effort and how you’re feeling, physically and emotionally. Hengehold also stresses mobility work, foam rolling, and stretching during this period.

One last thing no chatbot can do is look at your form. If you’re new to the weight room, Hengehold recommends having a gym friend or personal trainer check your technique early on: “Bad habits are hard to break and cause damage over time, and the same is true with your swimming, biking, and running.”

Yet technique is only part of what a generic plan misses.

“Triathletes are some of the most hardworking individuals on the planet and managing training, fatigue, and recovery requires extreme attention to detail,” Hengehold says. “The time, energy, and hard work need to be maximized to be worth it, which means a generalized strength plan will not meet the standard. Each athlete is a unique individual with individual needs that require an individualized plan.”

None of this is an argument against strength training — far from it. Hengehold calls it “absolutely essential to longevity in sport and health” and recommends it for every athlete. The argument is against spending your limited time and energy on a plan that wasn’t written with you in mind.

#8788. After 3 Marathons Without a Plan, I Finally Followed One. Here’s What Happened in NYC.

My 3:45 goal didn’t go to plan, but the NYC Marathon still delivered a win.

The first time I entered the New York City Marathon drawing, I got in. I’m not sure what possessed me that day to apply, having never run another race in my life. I figured I’d never get in, so why not? I played soccer growing up, and when the world shut down during COVID-19, running became the easiest way to get out of the house and see my friends. That’s where my running journey began.

My NYC Marathon training also happened during my senior year of college, which brought its own challenges. While I was excited to run, I also didn’t want to miss out on any of the socializing that happened that year. I did my best to make it to every party, every club soccer game, and anything in between while running as much as possible. I was scared that running was going to infringe on my everyday life and I wouldn’t have time to keep having fun. Despite all of that, I had caught the marathon bug and after finishing the New York City Marathon in 2022, I went on to run the Paris and Chicago Marathons in 2024.

While training for those first few marathons, I didn’t have any real plan, except to not let it interfere with my social calendar. My strategy consisted of building up mileage in order to reach 20 miles about four weeks out from race day. In between, I pieced together training information from influencers on Instagram and Google searches (this was pre-ChatGPT!). Now that I’m a Runner’s World+ member, I have all those resources right at my fingertips.

Although I caught the marathon bug almost instantly, I also felt defeated after New York. I knew I could have done better. Between New York City in 2022 and Paris in 2024, I never ran more than 10 miles at a time, but I was running enough that I knew I could do it again if I really wanted. I followed a similar approach for Chicago in 2024: Build up to one long run about a month out, then fill the rest of the weeks with shorter runs and one medium-length run. It wasn’t much of a plan, but it worked for me. My times kept improving, and I broke four hours for the first time in Chicago.

Looking back, I realize that my no-plan approach was partly a way to protect myself. If I never said my goal out loud, I couldn’t feel disappointed if I missed it. Breaking four hours in Chicago changed that. For the first time, I wanted to see what I could do with a real plan.

I was now living in the city I had expected to call home ever since I left college, so I really wanted this race to feel meaningful. For the first time in my marathon career, I downloaded a Runner’s World training plan, the 16-week Break 3:45 plan to be exact, printed it out, and started tracking all of my runs. I wanted to beat my time in Chicago and get as close to 3 hours and 45 minutes as possible.

In the beginning, this felt super daunting. I had never done an interval run in my life nor had I ever intentionally sought out hills to make my runs feel harder than they already did. Nonetheless, I found my old Garmin Forerunner 55 and learned how to upload intervals to run up and down the West Side Highway. When the plan called for hills, I made my way back to the Queensboro Bridge for the first time since 2022, ready to face it with excitement instead of fear. Even while pretending to be excited, the incline is no joke!

For a while, I really felt like I had gotten the hang of things. I actually started to recognize what different paces felt like during the intervals, instead of sprinting and pulling back and looking at my watch while I ran. And, I could now confidently run over many of the bridges in New York City, notably the Williamsburg and Manhattan, even though they aren’t even part of the marathon course. I wasn’t following the plan exactly, but I was able to reorganize the days of the week to hit all the workouts.

Near the end of August (roughly week eight of the plan), it became hot all the time, I was constantly traveling for weekend trips, and I had started to lose the excitement of running. So while I was making sure to hit all of the long runs, the interval training fell off completely. I was a little disappointed in myself because the interval training runs were workouts that made me feel like I was getting stronger each week. I had never done this type of workout before, so I could tell I was getting better each time.

To find the joy of running again, I really started to lean on my friends. Every week, I’d send out a few texts to see who was available and wanted to go for a run with me. I ran the loop in Central Park almost every week and met up with my friends in Brooklyn to run every Friday morning. I started to explore parts of the city I had never been to before, which helped ground me in my training and remember that running is supposed to be fun and is an exciting way to explore the city.

From my previous experience, I knew that running the long runs was the most important thing for me to feel confident on race day. So much of marathon running is mental, so knowing that I could run 20 miles (and have run 26.2 before), was enough for me. So, while I started with a plan, I started reverting back to my tried-and-true method—the just make sure you run the long runs plan.

Outside of the training plan itself, I leaned on Runner’s World a lot. I didn’t have access to this in the past so I didn’t feel confident about planning for prerun meals or even how to take gels during the race. I also found that being able to read runner stories online made me feel more connected to the community, which helped me mentally with my training.

Plan or no plan, I’m proud of myself! My official time was 3:57:39, so while I did not achieve my goal of breaking 3:45, I did run a sub-4 race, and following the Runner’s World plan helped me get there. The last time I ran this race, I was a senior in college and thought I had it all figured out. I was going to move to New York City, get a real adult job, and start the life I had been imagining. Similar to my experience following the Runner’s World plan, this is not how everything went. Instead, I moved to a different city after graduating, eventually found my way back to New York, and my life is so much more full than I ever expected because of it. Maybe things aren’t always supposed to go to plan, and that’s a good thing!

#8787. 12-Minute Calming Yoga to Gently Ease You Into Relaxation Mode

Ebony Smith, yoga instructor and founder of Yoga N Da Hood, offers a quick yin yoga practice to soothe the body and mind when you’re feeling anxious, overwhelmed, or simply need a break.

Even if anxiety is something you experience on the regular, you know that it can show up in completely expected ways throughout the day. Maybe you mentally replay a situation you wish you’d handled differently, or feel a sense of urgency to make more than one huge life decision in a single afternoon.

Yet sometimes the surest way to connect with yourself amid anxious tendencies is turning your attention to something that takes place in the here and now, rather than relates to the past or future. Such as stepping onto your yoga mat.

The following yin yoga practice is designed to help you relax and release tension, especially in your hips and lower back, by anchoring your body into the present moment—which can also encourage your mind to do the same. It’s a simple stretching practice that is quite restorative, especially when you feel apprehensive during the day or when you need some soothing before bed.

This sequence is made of supported yin yoga poses, slow breaths, and intentional pauses. No yoga experience needed. Simply find as quiet of a space as you can and, if possible, dim the lights. You can use a pillow, bolster, or block for extra support. Most yin yoga poses ask you to remain still for 3 to 5 minutes to create a stretch in the connective tissues. However, you can rest here for shorter amounts of time.

A little supine twist to get the party started. Lie on your back with your feet flat on the mat and your knees shining toward the ceiling. Take your arms straight out to the sides. Keep your feet on the mat as you lower both knees over toward the right. Turn your gaze over your left shoulder.

Stay here or, if it feels good, cross your left leg over your right. You can also place your right hand on your left thigh to gently intensify the stretch. To lessen the intensity, you can slide a pillow or bolster underneath your left knee. Notice where you might be holding any tension from the day and see if you can release it. Rest here for up to 3 minutes, then switch sides.

Lie on your back with your feet on the mat and your knees bent. Rest your arms by your sides and roll your shoulders underneath you. When you’re ready, press your feet into the mat and lift your hips toward the ceiling. Slide your block or bolster or pillows underneath your sacrum (the lowest part of your spine) in Supported Bridge Pose. Find a comfortable position, then rest here.

When you’re ready, remove the prop underneath you and lower your hips to the mat. Gently windshield wiper your knees side to side a few times.

Lie on your back with your feet on the mat and your knees bent. Take your feet wider, so they’re at the edge of the mat or a little outside the mat. Then relax your knees toward each other. They might rest against one another and they might not. Find a position in which you don’t have to use your muscles to hold your legs and you’re using gravity to draw your knees together. Take your arms out to the side or rest one hand over your heart and the other on your belly. Close your eyes if it feels good. Rest here.

From Constructive Rest, extend your legs long on the mat, maybe wiggling them out before finding stillness. Rest your arms by your sides. If it feels good, you can spread your palms out wide, shining them toward the ceiling. Close your eyes and begin to allow any stress, any worries, any fears, any doubts to melt off of you in Savasana. Notice yourself breathing in and out.

You can stay in Savasana for as long as it serves you. When you’re ready to come out of it, maybe wiggle your toes and fingers and stretch your arms overhead. Awaken to the amazing human being you truly are.

My friend Sean Mullaney, the FI Tax Guy, recently published an interesting article about the potential downsides of annuities. One of his observations is so simple that I think it's easy to overlook:

Most Americans already have an annuity. It's called Social Security.

Think about what an annuity is trying to accomplish. You give up some control over a pool of money in exchange for a predictable stream of income, often for the rest of your life. Social Security already provides lifetime income, with the added benefit of inflation adjustments.

For a married couple receiving substantial Social Security benefits, that could represent tens of thousands of dollars of annual income that they don't have to generate by selling investments.

#8785. The 12 Best Carbon Plate Shoes for Setting PRs, Running Your First Marathon, and Crossing the Finish Line Upright

From 5K to ultras, we logged race-day miles to see how these trainers performed in their element.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There are several max-cushioned shoes we recommend to carry you through hours of pounding pavement, but the true titans—composed of super foams sandwiching carbon-fiber plates—are listed here. There’s also a slew of new super shoes that made their debut this marathon cycle. We’ll update accordingly once these racers are available.

In 2017, Nike shook up running as we knew it with the unveiling of its Vaporfly 4%, a carbon plate marathon racing shoe that promised a 4 percent improvement in running economy (the measure of how fast you run based on the level of oxygen you use). Today, almost every shoe brand has a super shoe with a carbon plate and super foams, and they all make the same promise as the Vaporfly 4%: less energy expenditure while racing, or the ability to run faster with the same effort.

Here, we list the top performers based on wear-tester feedback and our own experiences racing in them. And if you’re in the market for other shoes to help you with your training, we have a buying guide for those too.

Your first marathon → Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)For a PR → Nike Alphafly 4 (Men’s/Women’s)But want to train in a plated shoe → New Balance SC Rebel (Men’s/Women’s)A flat and fast course → Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 (Unisex)A half marathon → Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo (Unisex)And want to try low drop → Altra Vanish Carbon 3 (Men’s/Women’s)And need support → Saucony Endorphin Pro 5 (Men’s/Women’s)And have wide feet → Hoka Cielo X1 3.0 (Unisex)On a track → Puma Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 (Men’s/Women’s)A 5K or 10K → New Balance SuperComp Elite v6 (Men’s/Women’s)On a trail → Hoka Tecton X 4 (Men’s/Women’s)An ultra → On Cloudultra Pro (Men’s/Women’s)

Besides our local testers, some of whom have been testing for us for the past 15 years, and staff who’ve also logged their share of road and trail time in these shoes, I have tested several of these shoes on race days. I have run 28 marathons since 2010, including 14 consecutive Boston Marathons. And I have made the split-second decision to race in new shoes marathon morning.

I’ve spoken with brand shoe development teams and have kept up with the latest super shoe releases. New shoes not listed here are still undergoing the testing process and will be added once feedback is in.

All of the shoes on this list were tested by local runners and Runner’s World staff. Our local testers include 300-plus men and women of various running experience levels, paces, arch heights, and gait patterns. From enthusiasts who run for fun to several Olympic-qualifying hopefuls, our mix of testers rounds out a sample of the overall running pop.

RW editors, including myself, have also raced in these shoes, from 5K to marathon distance (and some ultrarunners). We take into consideration fit, feel, and ride to determine the best racing shoes for almost every kind of runner hoping to PR, or just enjoy the propulsive experience of running on carbon plates sandwiched between super foams.

On a plane, running a shakeout run, and anytime a marathon was weeks away or days past, I’d hear first-timers and seasoned vets say the Adizero Adios Pro 4 was their race day shoe of choice. The latest iteration is sure to have the same mentions next race cycle.

I didn’t have the chance to race in the Adizero Adios Pro 5 yet, but I did try them out on my usual Central Park circuit in New York City. I was practically racing my casual loop after slurping half a can of beer (it was a long day on the job). It obviously wasn’t the kiwi-flavored Belgian White that had me clocking marathon pace (it got kinda funky after the 25th sip).

The carbon rim, which replaces the 4’s energy rods, is the secret sauce that subtracts weights and encourages a powerful snap that had me run up and down Harlem Hill like a gazelle. The Lightstrike Pro foam is also slightly firmer, which helps with high rebound and stability.

My only knock is how the rim shreds the hell of my ankle if my form gets slow and sloppy. But it’s a character trait. Senior Art Director Colin McSherry, for instance, ran his first marathon and had no issues—shoe- or first 26.2-related—during his run.

Shop Men’s at adidas.com | Shop Women’s at adidas.com

The Alphafly 3 went through some major changes to become more inclusive in terms of fit, weight, and ride. How do you update a shoe that was worn by the late Kelvin Kiptum, former marathon world record holder (2:00:35)? It starts with the Air units.

The ones in the Alphafly 4 are lighter and softer. During his testing, Runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate noted how the unit visibly squishes down when you stomp on the forefoot. The effect is a smoother, comfier ride with lots of pop.

The width of the shoe is also slightly wider (Nike really wants runners to stop saying their shoes are too unstable and narrow). Dengate noted how he didn’t have to slow down when turning corners.

The main critique is that loud clomping sound. But at this point—is it really an Alphafly if you can’t hear it coming up from behind you meters away?

Shop Men’s at nike.com | Shop Women’s at nike.com

The jury is still out on the pros and cons of solely training in super shoes, but we’re in the camp of keeping your special trainer fresh for race day. You can get a couple of runs in to troubleshoot and see if there are any issues pre-marathon or half, but I still urge runners to save the magic. But if you can’t get enough of that super foam, carbon plate high, enter the SC Rebel.

New Balance created this shoe specifically to make your training feel easier. It has the brand’s new TPEE-based Infinion foam, tuned for power runs, just like the SuperComp Elite v6 (New Balance’s premium racing shoe). It’s also an ideal alternative for racing if you need more stability. The shoe has a broader platform and grippy outsole that kept me upright on wet mud during a long run.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com

The Endorphin Elite 3 is as squishy and bouncy as its predecessor, but Saucony made the shoe more stable by connecting the forefoot and heel. Turns are less scary, but there’s still a learning curve to master the incredible energy return running in these shoes.

I tested them at a 5K and 3K in the Brooklyn Navy Yard, which was pocked with potholes and patched with slippery gravel. The shoes cut corners, but I still felt the need to slow down—or wipe out. I think on a more controlled runner’s feet these would make her feel powerful and unbeatable.

The source of that aggressive bounce is the TPEE-based IncrediRun foam. Its ride rivals even PEBA’s energy return.

The shoe also didn’t produce hot spots in the toe area. Saucony seems to have improved the fit with the third version. Once I wield this shoe’s power I won’t be afraid to run longer than a 10K. No friction here.

When I ran the Tokyo Marathon last year, I laced up in the Asics Metaspeed Sky Paris because I wanted more cushioning in the forefoot area. Asics recognized there are two ways of racing: stride running or cadence running. The Sky is intended for stride running: when you have a more powerful gait with longer strides and tend to strike on the midfoot.

At the Sydney Marathon this year, I opted for the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo instead. I felt the Edge would give me the, er, competitive edge, so to speak. My steps per minute are usually more than the average runner due to my mechanics and, well, because I’m short. The shoe has a scooped plate tilted slightly downward to cater to those with shorter steps (cadence running). I ended up hitting my sub-3:10 goal, finishing in 3:05.

The Edge Tokyo is updated with a softer underfoot, making the shoe more flexible. This makes the shoe have an incredible snap at toe-off. I was able to change gears at a fast clip when I latched onto a runner I was determined to pass (not always the best race strategy, but worked like a charm when I saw male runners try to overtake me).

Where competitors’ shoes have “air pods” or decoupled heels, the Metaspeeds provide runners with a simplified, choose-your-own-adventure super shoe that packs a powerful punch. One note for the wise: Because the Edge Tokyo has less firm cushioning, my heels and arches felt sore postrace. If you have heavy footfalls like me, have those recovery sandals waiting for you at bag check.

Shop Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at amazon.com

Altra started its journey into super shoes by staying true to itself. The Vanish Carbon 1 and 2 had wide toeboxes and were zero drop. But the Altra team knew there would have to be a compromise to go up against competitors’ shoes: the Vanish Carbon 3 needed a drop. The brand preserved the Altra way by adding just 4 mm (like the shoes in its Experience collection) to the heel with an aggressive rocker profile to promote propulsion.

Another Altra signature in the shoe is the roomy toebox that gives racers space to splay their toes, allowing them to engage their digits and power up during push-off.

The third iteration has pure PEBA midsole foam called FastRce. The foam provides more energy return and 2.6 percent improved running economy over the Vanish Carbon 2, which had a PEBA/EVA blend in its midsole.

The overall package presents a racer capable of racing against the other super shoes on this list.

The Endorphin Pro 5 has a more stable ride than its springier sibling, the Endorphin Elite 2, which we also included on this list.

Its midsole is dual-layer PEBA, with one layer Pwrrun PB and the other layer Pwrrun HG. These layers provide a high-rebound ride and work with the rocker Speedroll tech to encourage fast, smooth turnover.

Testers like the shoe’s propulsive ride as well as support throughout their workouts.

“What stood out most was the combination of propulsion and stability,” said tester Srah Pezzino. “The carbon plate paired with Saucony’s Pwrrun HG foam delivers a responsive, fast ride without feeling unstable or overly bouncy. This helped immensely during longer tempo runs when fatigue starts to creep in. I felt like the shoe encouraged good mechanics and smooth turnover rather than forcing speed.

“Compared to previous carbon-plated shoes I’ve worn, the Pro 5 feels more predictable and controlled, especially when my form isn’t perfect late in a run. It’s a shoe that makes you feel fast without punishing you for not being perfectly locked in.”

Shop Men’s at saucony.com | Shop Women’s at saucony.com

The lightest Hoka marathon racing shoe yet is the Cielo X1 3.0, with street cred at the 2025 Chicago Marathon. Hoka-sponsored pro-runner Alex Masai raced in a blacked-out prototype of the shoe, shaved nearly four minutes off his personal best time, and podiumed third with a 2:04:37 finish.

And our testers clocked the shoe’s massive updates, as well. “The 3.0 is sturdier than the 2.0,” said tester Mike Browne. “I’m referring to the sturdiness mainly on heel strikes. I wore the 2.0 during marathon training and in a marathon, and they actually underpronated a little. I think that is what caused the outside heel rubber to come off on both shoes. The 3.0 has corrected that issue and seems to strike the ground in the center, which makes for a more even wear on the shoe.”

Besides implementing a lighter upper, the Hoka team redesigned the midsole shape, creating a long channel that runs down the center of the shoe. The rocker also isn’t as exaggerated. What you get is a more stable, smoother ride while racing with propulsion that’s comparable to Hoka’s competitors’. The fit is also broader in the midfoot, making the Cielo X1 3.0 a good choice for runners with wide feet.

The Fast-R Nitro Elite 3 is a prime pick for marathon racing, but it’s also a solid choice for everything else under 26.2 miles. The shoe is so lightweight and delivers such explosive rebound—“you feel like you’re running straight down a trampoline,” says a tester—that it left some of us feeling like we had brownie batter for legs after hard efforts.

The shoe was the talk of the industry prelaunch after Puma released a study (which the brand sponsored) comparing the Fast-R Nitro Elite 3’s performance to the Nike Alphafly 3, Adidas Adios Pro Evo 1, and Puma Fast-R 2. The study claimed the Elite 3 was 3.15 to 3.62 percent more economical than its competitors.

Putting those numbers aside, our testers agreed this is one powerful racing shoe. “The foam used in this shoe is very noticeable, even when simply starting with a short warmup in the shoe,” says tester Codi Januszkiewicz, who compares the ride to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4. “Accelerating from a warmup pace straight into some speedwork intervals felt smooth; somehow moving faster in this shoe felt even easier than the warmup.”

But that power is a lot to handle. “The stability is lacking,” says tester Sean O’Connor. “Almost felt high heelish to me, and it jacked up my calves and feet a little as well. When I ran in them it felt like I was perpetually holding onto the shoe with my feet. I think that's why it made my calves and feet sore.”

Some can handle the shoe’s intensity over a long period of time. Others may assign the Elite 3 as their mid-distance racing shoe instead. I wore the Elite 3 at a Trackmith 5000 meters over the summer, hitting a PR at 19:12. It’s cush in the heel, but judging by my footfalls, which are heavy, I think racing them in a 26.2 would prolong my usual recovery time postrun.

When I raced the 2025 London Marathon, I had been training in the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v4 but instead opted for the FuelCell SuperComp Pacer v2. The Pacer is sleeker and lightweight, unlike the SuperComp Elite v4, which was too beefy for my small frame. The SuperComp Elite v6 is the version of the shoe I would have raced in. Unfortunately, I can’t go back to April 2025. Fortunately for you, the Elite v6 is here just in time for fall marathon season.

The shoe features the brand’s Infinion foam, which was introduced in the 1080v15. The Elite v6’s version of the TPEE- and TPU-based foam is dialed-in for race-ready energy return.

I took the shoe out on a track for a 2 x 2-mile workout at 6:45 pace and the shoes handled turns and helped me hit goal pace. The ride isn’t as aggressive as the Saucony Endorphin Elite 3 or Alphafly, and the cushioning is firmer. Runners with an efficient stride and good form can get away with running marathons and halfs in these shoes, but I’d recommend these for 5Ks and 10Ks because of the firmness and less explosive rebound. The lighter weight makes it ideal for track and medium-distance road races.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com

Though I’ve been racing for 20 years, nothing will get me running an ultra on the trail—which is where our Senior Editor Cat Bowen comes in. Bowen conquered scrambles on steep climbs, dusty ridgelines, gnarly technical trails, and more types of terrain than I run in a year, while testing the long-awaited Tecton X 4.

She gave a shoutout to the hardy Matryx upper that’s “tough as nails” and the grippy 4mm lugs that prevented her from plunging forward. The plus/minus with the shoe is that built-in gaiter collar. Bowen appreciated the extra coverage, but lamented how difficult it was to put on the shoe (we get it: a side zipper would be a good cheat but adds weight). “There is absolutely no reason why this shoe has a front pull tab and nothing in the back,” she wrote in her review.

Still, the new cushioning, Hoka’s ProFly X, and non-winged plate make for a more energized ride that’s less rigid without losing stability. It’s a great shoe for unpredictable. but Bowen urges you to not go the no-sock route.

Shop Men’s at hoka.com | Shop Women’s at hoka.com

For hours, days, weeks on the trail, there’s the Cloudultra Pro. Bowen has gone through three pairs of the shoe—not because they lack durability but because she likes them so much and runs that much—and appreciates how she doesn’t have to slice the sides. Feet swell during ultras, but it sounds like On prepared for that with its roomy but secure upper.

Another plus in Bowen’s column of ultra shoe musts is the Cloudultra Pro’s lateral stability. Maneuvering over rugged, uneven terrain could spell twisted ankles and slipping and sliding, but the shoe didn’t lead Bowen astray.

Ultrarunner Pat Heine-Holmberg also wore the shoe around Germany’s Zugspitze, where he raced the 102-mile ZUT1000 and ran on “every surface imaginable.”

Shop Men’s at on.com | Shop Women’s at on.com

Brands are now beginning to release carbon shoes in men’s and women’s sizes. Still, in some cases there’s not much difference between the types of shoes except for maybe the sizing and colors. If the shoes are unisex, it may take a few try-ons to get the fit right. In my unisex racing shoe experience, I’ve found the collar can be loose while the midfoot can be tight. You may want to size up or down, and adopt the heel-lock tying method if the heel area feels too loose.

Do all carbon-fiber plates behave the same way? Sort of. An important lesson to learn here is that the plate isn’t the secret sauce of super shoes—it doesn’t cause propulsion. Instead, the plate, sandwiched between the highly responsive foams, acts as a stabilizer to the super foam. This is why super shoes have such tall stack heights, and why World Athletics caps racing shoe stack height at 40 mm. The super foam—and amount underfoot—is a major advantage.

When choosing a carbon-plate shoe, you’ll want to consider what you’re using it for—racing on the road or trail—and, if possible, have your gait evaluated to determine the best plate angle if you’re looking at shoes specific to running type.

Some plates are full-length or have cutouts. In shoes like the Asics Metaspeed Edge and Metaspeed Sky, the plate’s angle differentiates running types. The Edge’s plate dips lower in the forefoot so cadence runners can roll off their toes faster. The Sky’s plate sits flat in the forefoot, allowing stride runners to leverage bounce on longer steps.

The secret sauce in super shoes is the foam. PEBA (polyether block amide) was once considered the holy grail of all foams and you can still find it in most super shoes, but newer models are using TPEE (thermoplastic polyester elastomer) and A-TPU (aliphatic thermoplastic polyurethane) because they’re more resistant to bottoming out, or going flat. The ride is more durable—and can be quite aggressively bouncy and squishy.

To truly gauge which foam is best for you, trying on the shoe and giving it a run (preferably with some cornering) will help you determine if you want a firmer or squishier ride.

A carbon-fiber plate shoe is an investment, costing anywhere from $240 upward of $500. There are a couple of things to take into account on a personal level before buying: Can you afford a trainer that’s less durable compared to the standard workhorse shoe, which lasts between 450 to 500 miles?

While these super shoes are more durable than the ones made eight years ago, they still have a shorter shelf life due to high-performance foams—PEBA and supercritical blends—wearing down faster. Lastly, is the return there? While brands claim these shoes can improve performance, it’s not guaranteed your running economy will improve by around 4 percent.

I spoke with Ted Fitzpatrick, Saucony’s VP of product management, about the differences. He made these key points between carbon and nylon plates:

A nylon plate is semirigid with some flexibility. A carbon plate is rigid with little or no flexibility. Popsicle analogy—Imagine the plate as the stick that holds the soft ice cream together. The fundamental use of the plates is to keep the dimensional stability of the foam. With each type of plate, each offers different levels of compliance. The plate maintains the forward rolling effect of super shoes. Carbon is the stiffest, which offers the most concentrated effect of speed roll technology. Nylon still adds stiffness, however, it offers better compliance in how the foot transitions in the gait cycle. Some individuals can respond better to different plates. It is down to what works best for the user.

Saucony offers the nylon-plated Endorphin Speed 6, a training shoe that complements its racer, the Endorphin Pro. The shoe can also serve as a more affordable racing shoe, at $180. (The Endorphin Elite 3 and Endorphin Pro 5 cost $290 and $240.)

“The foam is what does the heavy lifting of a super shoe, however it’s the plate that guides how each foam behaves to the user,” says Fitzpatrick. “It is best to train in both to strengthen and build ‘muscle memory’ into different muscle groups.”

However, we wouldn’t recommend solely training in super shoes. For one thing, it would be extremely expensive to use these shoes as daily trainers when they have a shorter shelf life compared to standard everyday shoes. We advise going on a couple of runs before racing in the shoes, to get used to running in them and check for hot spots. While running constantly in these shoes won’t necessarily lead to injury, overuse and the desire to run faster in carbon shoes will likely lead to getting sidelined if you’re not careful.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.
